name: Gum contouring laser

lead: Laser gum contouring evens out the gum line and shows more tooth, using a dental laser instead of a scalpel to trim soft tissue. It is a laser form of gingivectomy.

The laser vaporizes and cuts gum tissue while sealing small vessels, leaving a reshaped, balanced gum line once healed. Wikipedia lists Nd:YAG, CO2 and diode lasers among those used and notes proposed benefits such as a bloodless field and minimal discomfort, based on limited evidence. Few registered studies look at it directly.

paras: A dentist trims the gum in a short visit, and the reshaped gum line is visible after healing. It is often used alongside other smile work such as veneers or whitening.

High energy settings were linked to scarring and delayed healing in animal studies. As with other gum trimming, removed tissue does not simply grow back, and the claimed advantages over a scalpel rest on limited evidence.

angle.text: Laser gum contouring is used to even out the gum line and show more tooth, as a laser version of gingivectomy. The laser trims gum tissue and the reshaped gum line is visible after healing. Few studies look at the laser technique directly.

lead: Laser gum contouring reshapes the gum line using a dental laser to remove soft tissue, a form of laser gingivectomy.[1] Wikipedia lists Nd:YAG, CO2 and diode lasers among those used, and notes proposed benefits such as a bloodless field and minimal discomfort, based on limited evidence.[1]

Few registered studies address it directly. One compares Er:YAG-assisted laser crown lengthening with surgical crown lengthening,[2] and another examined wound-healing growth factors after soft tissue crown lengthening.[3]

paras: The laser removes gum tissue; the procedure involves repeated lasing and wiping debris, producing a bloodless field and removing the need for a dressing.[1]
Animal studies suggest high energy settings cause scarring and delayed healing, and the evidence on lasers is described as mixed.[1]

Registered trials include a phase 2 study of growth factor levels during wound healing after soft tissue crown lengthening (n=80)[3] and a comparison of Er:YAG laser versus surgical crown lengthening (n=26, recruiting).[2] No results are summarised in the sources used.
